title: The Komagata Maru, 1914
hookLine: a ship of mostly Sikh passengers is turned away at Vancouver and returns to violence in India
last: A DOOR IN A NEW LAND.

cards: May 1914. A Japanese steamship sails into Vancouver harbor, its rails lined with men in turbans, looking at the city.
Three hundred seventy-six passengers, most of them Sikh, all of them British subjects of the same empire as Canada. They've come to work, like the mill men before them. The ship drops anchor.
Then nothing happens. Nobody is allowed off. Days pass, then weeks, and the city watches from the shore.

teach.b: Remember the rule that closed Canada's door: immigrants had to arrive by a continuous journey from home, and no ships ran straight from India. A Sikh businessman named Gurdit Singh decided to test it.

He chartered a ship, the Komagata Maru, filled it with passengers from Punjab, and gave it a new name: Guru Nanak Jahaz, the Guru Nanak ship. At Vancouver, the authorities refused to let the passengers land.
The ship sat in the harbor for two months, and food and water ran low. Vancouver's Sikhs, those mill workers, raised money to help and fought in the courts. They lost.
Only about twenty passengers, mostly returning residents, were allowed in. In July, with a navy ship standing by, the Komagata Maru was forced to sail away.
When it reached India, near Calcutta, in September 1914, British police met it. The passengers were ordered onto a train to Punjab; many refused.
There was a confrontation, shots were fired, and around twenty passengers were killed. Others were imprisoned.
For decades, Sikhs in Canada kept the memory alive with plaques, books, and a memorial on the Vancouver waterfront, near where the ship once waited.
In 2016, Canada's Prime Minister stood in the House of Commons and apologized.
It matters because they were turned away not for anything they did, but for who they were and where they were from.

how: Sikhs in Canada remember the Komagata Maru each year, with Ardas and gatherings at the Vancouver memorial, and tell the story to their children as part of the community's history.

games.q: you're Gurdit Singh in 1914. Canada says immigrants must come by a continuous journey, and no such ships run from India. what do you do?
o: accept the rule and stay home.
charter a ship and sail straight to Vancouver.
go to the United States instead.
games.why: he chartered the Komagata Maru to test the rule. the passengers were still refused, and the ship was forced away.

practice: Think of someone new in your life: a new neighbor, a coworker, a new kid in class, someone who just joined a group you're in. Picture what it's like to be them right now, standing at the edge, not sure if they're wanted.
Then picture yourself walking over, and quietly rehearse the one simple thing you'd say.

wordCard.voice: Komagata Maru. In 1914, a ship of mostly Sikh passengers waited two months at Vancouver, was turned away, and met violence on its return to India.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Guru Nanak jahaz, the Guru Nanak ship, Gurdit Singh's name for the Komagata Maru.
